title: Value — the engine's currency
summary: Everything downstream of the trace loader speaks one type: `mch::Value`. A matcher's `where` expression, a parsed message body, a build program's capture, a host function's return, an Action column — all of them are Values, and every equality, render and null-check in this tutorial is a rule about this one struct. It is a hand-discriminated tagged union of 14 kinds with a deliberately Python-shaped semantics: unbounded integers (`RefInt256`, because jetton amounts overflow int64), an `Amount` wrapper that can be present-but-empty (`Amount(None)`), an `Account` that can be present-but-addr_none, and two different map kinds that differ only in attribute-access rules. Read this chapter for four things you will otherwise re-derive painfully later: why `null` and `addr_none` are not the same value (and why the two parser universes disagree about which one a missing address becomes), why Cell-derived fields are compared by root hash instead of bytes, why there are two equality functions rather than one, and why the `VType` enum may only ever be appended to.

sections.heading: What a Value is, and why the enum only grows
sections.prose:
`Value.h` opens with the only design rationale you get for the whole model, and it is worth reading as a spec rather than as a comment: each bullet is a Python behaviour that had to be imported rather than improved on. The C++ side is a mirror of what `indexer/events/mch/expr_eval.py` produces, and the twin gates compare RENDERED values ([[gates]]) — so every place the two could disagree had to be decided deliberately, once, here.

The `VType` enum carries an unwritten rule that the design docs state explicitly: it is APPEND-ONLY. `W12-BRIDGE-DESIGN.md` §3 rejects a native external-address kind on exactly this ground — "Value.h VType enum is append-only and adding a member forces a clean engine-obj rebuild". The hazard is mechanical, not stylistic: several translation units in this engine are GENERATED into the build tree (`wheres_generated.cpp`, `builds_ir_generated.cpp`, …) and ninja will happily reuse their stale object files after a `Value` layout or enum change, producing a binary whose halves disagree about the struct — which shows up as heap corruption at runtime, not as a link error. Inserting a member in the middle of the enum is the worse version of the same bug, because generated code stores kind tags.

excerpts.title: Value.h — the four decisions everything else inherits

annotations.text: Every expression integer is a 256-bit big-int, not an int64, and that is a correctness requirement rather than caution: Python ints are unbounded and a jetton amount routinely exceeds int64. Widening happens on entry (JSON numbers, host fields), so no arithmetic path in the engine ever has to think about overflow — but it also means `num` is a refcounted handle that can be NULL, and a null `num` is meaningful (see the `Amount` line in the kind list below, and `make_amount_none`).

The distinction the rest of this chapter keeps returning to: `Account` has a third state besides "has an address" and "is absent" — present-but-empty (`addr_none`). It mirrors `AccountId(None)`, whose `repr` is `addr_none` but whose `as_str()` is None. A null Value and an addr_none Account are different values and compare unequal.

A parity bug faithfully preserved: Python's `Asset.__eq__` reads the jetton master's string BEFORE it checks the `is_ton` branch, so comparing a TON asset with a string raises instead of matching "ton". The C++ side reproduces the raise as a fault, and the dead `"ton"` branch stays dead. Fixing this would be an A/B diff, not a bug fix ([[gates]]).

`Dict` and `Obj` carry the same payload and differ ONLY in attribute-access semantics — `Obj` is a `SimpleNamespace` (message envelope, parsed body, lookup record) and gets the `.exit_code` envelope accessor; `Dict` is a plain map (block data, record literal). Because they are distinct kinds, a Dict never compares equal to an Obj with identical fields.

Containers are shared, never copied — which is only safe because a Value is immutable once built. There is no mutating API on `Value` anywhere in the engine; a "changed" object is a new `make_obj` over rebuilt fields.

A Value can point at a matched `Block` — the tree from [[block-tree]] — through a raw non-owning pointer. That works because blocks live in an arena that outlives every Value derived from it, per trace. It also means Block-valued equality is pointer identity (mirroring Python's default `__eq__`), not structural.

APPEND-ONLY. Adding `Foo` at the end costs a clean rebuild of the engine objects; inserting it in the middle silently renumbers every kind tag baked into already-compiled generated TUs. When the ABI bridge needed a representation for external addresses it built an `Obj{bits,value}` rather than pay this ([[parse-layer]]).

`Amount` is not a synonym for `Int`: it is a wrapper kind whose payload may be null (`Amount(None)`), and `Account` is not a synonym for `Str`. Both exist so that Python's wrapper types survive the round trip into the dumps — collapsing either one would make the twin comparison lossy.

`Float` exists only because fixture data contains one (a GetGems price). The language has no floats — but the fault is narrower than "any use": a float-backed AMOUNT (same `dnum`, `amount_float` set) faults on `==`, on arithmetic and on `.value`, the three pinned vectors; a BARE Float faults on arithmetic and attribute access, yet an `==` against it merely returns false, because the guard tests `t == Amount && amount_float` and a Float slips past it into `container_eq`. Rendering is split too: `BuildDriver` prints `float:<%.17g>` (the line's "bare -> unrenderable" comment predates that), while `describe()` and `--parse-dump` still print `?`. A dead end by design either way, not an escape hatch.

sections.heading: The struct: one flat bag, hand-discriminated
sections.prose:
There is no `std::variant` here. Every kind's payload is a named member of one struct, and only the members relevant to `t` are meaningful. That is a deliberate trade — it keeps the type trivially copyable-ish and cheap to pass around, at the cost that nothing prevents you from reading `str` off an `Int`. When you read engine code, always check `t` first; `v.str` on the wrong kind is empty rather than wrong-looking.

The factories below are the ONLY sanctioned way to build a Value (plus the default-constructed `null()`), and several of them encode a contract that the struct itself cannot: `make_account_raw` takes an ALREADY-normalized string, `make_amount_none` deliberately leaves `num` null, `make_amount_float` sets a flag that makes the value un-usable in expressions.

annotations.text: `dnum` is shared by two kinds and `amount_float` is what tells them apart: an Amount whose payload is a Python float keeps `num` NULL and its value in `dnum`. That collision is exactly why `amount_none()` in [[build-programs]]'s runtime has to exclude float-backed amounts — otherwise a float price would silently compare equal to `Amount(None)`.

One `str` member serves four kinds: text, raw bytes, the canonical account address, and the jetton master of an Asset. Bytes are held as a `std::string` of raw octets (not text) — which is why the dumps base64 them on the way out rather than printing them.

Three booleans encode the sub-states that make `Account` and `Asset` more than strings: addr_none, TON-vs-jetton, and jetton-master-present. `is_ton=true, has_jetton=false` is the TON asset — and it is the state that faults when compared against a string (`ExprRuntime.cpp:166`). The only two Asset factories produce TON (true/false) or jetton (false/true), so false/false is unreachable; that is why `!has_jetton` ALONE is a safe test for "there is no master string to compare".

`items` and `fields` are `shared_ptr` so a Value stays cheap to copy; `block` is a bare pointer with no ownership at all. The arena-outlives-values invariant behind that pointer is the one lifetime rule in the value model — a Value must never outlive the trace whose blocks it references ([[block-tree]]).

`Amount(None)`: a present Amount carrying nothing. Its documented behaviour — "== only to itself" — is what a spec relies on when a protocol legitimately has no amount yet; it is NOT null, so `x == null` is false for it.

"caller normalized" is a real contract with no enforcement: pass a lowercase or malformed address here and it silently becomes a value that will never compare equal to a properly built one. Every call site pairs this with `normalize_raw_address` (below) — that pairing IS the invariant.

The entire read API: an `is_null` predicate and one field lookup. There are no getters per kind — consumers switch on `t` and read the member directly, which is why the members above are public and why reading the wrong one is possible.

`describe()` is diagnostic-first (FAIL lines, fault messages) — it is not the PRIMARY dump rendering. The comparable renders live in `ParseDump.cpp` and `BuildDriver.cpp` and are deliberately different formats. One caveat: `ParseDump`'s `render_value` ends in `default: return v.describe();`, so for the kinds it does not case on — List, Block, Float — `describe()` IS the de-facto `--parse-dump` render (and, having no Float case, it prints `?` for one of them).

sections.heading: Field access: Dict, Obj, and the `.exit_code` hop
sections.prose:
Both map kinds store a `vector<pair<string, Value>>`, not a `std::map`. The reason is size, not order: field counts are tiny, so a linear scan beats a node-per-key tree and the whole Fields vector is a single allocation.

Insertion order is PRESERVED but almost nowhere observable. Every comparable render sorts keys — `render_fields_sorted` in `ParseDump.cpp`, the explicit key sort in `BuildDriver.cpp`, and `sorted(...)` in both Python twins — and neither equality function is order-sensitive (`structural_equal` and `container_eq` both compare key SETS). What genuinely sees insertion order is `describe()`, the positional assertions in `DexRecordsTest.cpp` (`key_at(d, 0, "asset")` and friends), and the ABI bridge's rule that `"$"` is emitted FIRST so a consumer can switch on `.$` (`W12-BRIDGE-DESIGN.md` §3, Struct row).

The lookup itself is trivial; the interesting behaviour is one level up, in the expression runtime's `rt_access`, which is where the Dict/Obj distinction finally pays for itself.

annotations.text: A Value whose kind has no fields carries a null `fields` shared_ptr, so `field()` answers "absent" instead of dereferencing null — the lookup is TOTAL over all 14 kinds. Note that every caller in the engine still switches on `t` first anyway (`structural_equal`, `container_eq`, `rt_access`, `BuildDriver`); the totality is a safety net, not an idiom.

First match wins, so a Fields vector with a duplicate key is not an error — it shadows. Nothing in the engine builds one today, but a parser that `emplace_back`s the same name twice would produce a value whose second entry is unreachable by lookup yet still counted by every size-based comparison (see `structural_equal` and `container_eq` below, both of which compare `size()` first).

excerpts.title: rt_access — where Dict and Obj stop being the same thing

annotations.text: Null PROPAGATES through attribute access — `x.a.b` on a null `x` is null, never a fault. This is the single most load-bearing null rule in the language: it is why an unparsed body (`.body` null after a failed parse, [[parse-layer]]) makes a whole guard expression evaluate to null rather than blow up.

The one accessor that is not a lookup: `.exit_code` on an Obj hops through the envelope's `transaction` sub-object to `compute_exit_code`. Note the asymmetry — a missing `transaction` FAULTS (you asked a message-envelope question of a non-envelope), but a transaction without the field yields null (the transaction genuinely had no compute phase).

A MISSING field is a fault, not null — the opposite of the null-propagation rule two lines above. Absent-key means the spec is wrong about the shape; null-object means the data was absent. Keeping those distinguishable is why `Value::field` returns a pointer instead of an optional-Value.

Dict and Obj reach identical code here — only the fault MESSAGE differs ("object" vs "data"). The kinds are kept distinct for equality and for the `.exit_code` envelope rule, not because plain lookup behaves differently.

sections.heading: Accounts, and the two meanings of nothing
sections.prose:
An address enters the engine as text from three directions — a transaction account off the trace loader, a parsed message field, an address literal in a spec — and all three funnel through `normalize_raw_address` before becoming an `Account`. Canonical form is raw `wc:HEX` with UPPERCASE hex, matching Python's `AccountId.as_str()`. User-friendly base64 addresses are simply not a thing in this engine.

The important part is what happens to a MISSING address, because the two parser universes answer differently. On the pytoniq-parity path an `addr_none` in a message body becomes a NULL Value; on the ABI path it becomes `Value::make_account_none()` — a present Account with `addr_none` set ([[parse-layer]]). Both are correct for their own twin, and the run below shows the pytoniq answer landing in a real dump. A spec that null-tests an address field is therefore asking a question whose meaning depends on which parser produced it.

One more asymmetry worth internalising: the `account()` builtin FAULTS on a string it cannot normalize (and maps the literal string `"addr_none"` to `make_account_none()`), while the trace-side helper passes a non-normalizable address through unchanged rather than failing the trace.

excerpts.title: normalize_raw_address — the canonicalization every comparison depends on

annotations.text: Parsing is deliberately narrow: exactly one colon-separated raw form. There is no base64 branch, no bounce-flag handling, no testnet variant — the vectors never use them, and adding one would silently change what compares equal.

Exactly 64 hex digits — no zero-padding of a short account id, no truncation of a long one. A 63-digit address is rejected rather than repaired, so a malformed address becomes a visible fault (via the builtin) instead of a value that quietly matches nothing.

Uppercasing is the whole point of the function: `Account` equality is a plain `str ==` (no case folding anywhere), so canonicalization at construction is what makes two addresses from different sources comparable at all. Contrast `Asset`-vs-string equality, which DOES lowercase both sides at compare time — an inconsistency inherited from Python, not a choice made here.

The workchain is validated as an optional `-` plus digits and then carried through as TEXT, not parsed to an int: `-1:AB..` and `-01:AB..` normalize to different strings and will not compare equal. Nothing produces the padded form today, which is why this has never bitten.

excerpts.title: The trace-side constructor — normalize, but never fail

annotations.text: An ABSENT address (no `optional`) becomes null — not addr_none. This is the trace-loader convention and it matches the pytoniq parser convention, which is why null-testing works consistently for everything except ABI-parsed bodies.

A non-normalizable address is passed through RAW rather than rejected. Deliberate: the loader must not fail a whole trace over one odd account string, so the bad value survives as an Account that simply never matches. The `account()` builtin makes the opposite choice and faults — spec authors get told, the ingest path does not.

sections.heading: Cells: the root hash is the currency
sections.prose:
A `Cell` Value is a `td::Ref<vm::Cell>` and compares by root hash everywhere. The subtler rule is about cell-derived STRINGS and BYTES: a `forward_payload` that a parser serialized to BOC bytes, or a `b64()` builtin output, cannot be compared bytewise between the two engines — pytoniq and td produce different BOC containers (ordering, CRC provenance) for the same cell tree. Plan §12 resolves this by rendering such fields as `cellhash:<HEX-UPPER>` in every comparable dump.

The gate is by FIELD NAME, not by value type — `is_boc_field("forward_payload")` is true, `is_boc_field("comment")` is false — because `comment`, `bitcoin_txid` and `pubkey` are raw non-BOC bytes whose exact bytes ARE the data. That set is small, hand-curated, and exported to the Python twins through `--surface` so a name can never be in the set on one side only.

(`td_boc_serialize`, just above the excerpt, is the other half of the same decision: once dumps compare by root hash, container byte order stops mattering, so the engine uses td's deterministic native writer everywhere. The former pytoniq-order writer — and a P3 exponential-re-walk DoS in it — went away with that change.)

excerpts.title: The free functions Value.h exports — BOC-field rendering, address normalization, harness equality (three concerns, six declarations)

annotations.text: Read this as the definition of the root-hash bar: it is a RENDERING rule, applied at dump time, not a change to how values are stored or compared in the runtime. Two engines can hold different BOC bytes for the same tree and still produce identical dumps.

Name-gated, and surfaced. `--surface` prints this set as JSON; the twins then load the COMMITTED `twins/cpp_surface.json` snapshot through `cpp_surface.py` and re-export it as `BOC_FIELDS`, instead of each hand-mirroring a literal. Regenerating that snapshot is a manual step, so the twin CAN go stale — a stale one is caught downstream by the classify/parse A/B gates and `tests/mch/test_ir_emit.py`, not prevented ([[gates]]).

"`addr_none` is NOT handled here" is the boundary that keeps this function total and boring: it answers only "is this a well-formed raw address", and the three-state Account logic lives in the callers.
Flagged loudly as NOT the `==` operator — the split this chapter's last section is about. `structural_equal` is the conformance-vector comparator and has exactly two callers, both in the harness.

excerpts.title: The BOC-field set and its renderer (57 lines — the set and the function that consumes it only make sense read together)

annotations.text: The whole set: seven names, all of them fields whose value is a serialized cell tree. The exclusions in the comment are the interesting part — `comment` is UTF-8 text bytes and `bitcoin_txid` / `pubkey` are fixed-width binary, so hashing them would destroy the very content the twins are trying to compare.

Three accepted input shapes for the same logical thing: an actual Cell, raw BOC Bytes (what a pytoniq-path parser produces for a payload), and a base64 Str (what the `b64()` builtin produces). All three collapse to the same hash — which is exactly the point, since the two engines choose different ones for the same field.

The failure marker is itself designed to be A/B-comparable: both engines derive the 12-char prefix from the same source (the b64 string, or base64 of the raw bytes), so even a corrupt BOC field would diff cleanly instead of producing engine-specific noise. It has never fired over the corpus.

An empty return means "not renderable as a cellhash — fall back to the normal render", and it is used for a null cell and for any other kind. That protocol is why every call site is the two-line `if (rendered.empty())` pattern rather than a single expression.
Hex is uppercased by hand rather than via `to_hex` — the render string is compared bytewise against Python's `v.hash.hex().upper()`, so case is data, not formatting.

excerpts.title: The dump render — where the distinctions become visible text

annotations.text: `Int` and `Amount` render IDENTICALLY (bare decimal): the wrapper distinction that matters so much to equality is invisible in this dump. Note also the unguarded `v.num->` — a parsed Amount always carries a value here, but this render would crash on an `Amount(None)`, which is why it is a parse-dump renderer and not a general one.

Bytes render as their FULL base64, compared raw — because for a non-BOC byte field pytoniq and td agree exactly. Fields in the BOC set never reach this branch: `render_fields_sorted` (just above) checks `is_boc_field` on the KEY first and substitutes the cellhash.

The null/addr_none distinction survives all the way into the comparable text: an absent address prints `null` (from the Null case at the top), a present-but-empty one prints `addr_none`. This is the line that makes the two parser universes' disagreement visible in a diff.

A bare `Cell` Value always renders by hash regardless of field name — the name gate only exists for the string/bytes forms, where the value alone cannot tell you whether it is a BOC container or raw data.

runs.note: `fns` / `parsers` / `preds` trimmed — the line that belongs to this chapter is `boc_fields`, the exact set from `boc_field_names()`. Redirecting this output into `twins/cpp_surface.json` is how the Python side gets `BOC_FIELDS`: `cpp_surface.py` reads the committed snapshot, so the twins hash the same seven names — as of the last regeneration.

sections.heading: Two equalities, on purpose
sections.prose:
There are two deep-equality functions over `Value` and they are kept apart deliberately. `structural_equal` (in `Value.cpp`) is the HARNESS comparator: it answers "does this actual value match the expected value from a conformance vector", and it is asymmetric — the EXPECTED value's type drives the switch. `rt_eq` → `raw_eq` → `container_eq` (in `ExprRuntime.cpp`) is the LANGUAGE's `==`: symmetric, with cross-type rules (Account vs Str, Asset vs Str) that a harness comparator has no business having.

The file comment states the reasoning plainly: "the runtime owns its own container `==` instead of borrowing the harness comparator… The two are behaviourally equivalent for the value model today — this is a separation of concerns so `structural_equal` stays harness-only." Read that claim narrowly, because it is scoped to the CONTAINER walks — and those do agree. The GUARDS in front of them do not: `eq_result` faults on a float-backed Amount, and on TON-asset-vs-string, before `raw_eq` is ever reached, whereas `structural_equal` quietly accepts the first of those pairings. The separation is what lets a change to what a spec's `==` means avoid silently changing what a vector accepts. If you are reading match/build behaviour, `rt_eq` is the one you want ([[build-programs]]); if you are reading a FAIL line from `--vectors`, it came from `structural_equal` ([[gates]]).

annotations.text: `switch (b.t)` — the EXPECTED value's kind selects the rule and the actual must then match it. That asymmetry is correct for a vector runner (it mirrors the Python runner's `_equal`) and wrong for a language operator, which is the entire reason for the split.

`Amount(None) == Amount(None)` and nothing else — note it tests `num.is_null()` on both sides, so a float-backed Amount (also null `num`) compares equal to `Amount(None)` HERE. The runtime refuses that pairing with a fault instead; a case where the two equalities genuinely differ, and it is safe only because vectors never expect a float-backed Amount.
addr_none pairs only with addr_none, and otherwise it is a plain string compare — no normalization at compare time. Whatever `normalize_raw_address` did at construction is final.
The first of the two internal recursions. List is element-wise and POSITIONAL — for a list, order IS data, unlike the map kinds two cases down.

The second recursion, and the one that makes the harness comparator order-independent: each key of the EXPECTED map is looked up by name in the actual. Note it recurses into `structural_equal`, not into the language's `raw_eq` — so nested scalars get plain type-checked equality with none of the Account-vs-Str / Asset-vs-Str cross-type rules (contrast `container_eq` below, which is the same walk wired to the other comparator).

Where an expected Float lands: there is no `case VType::Float` anywhere in the switch, so it falls off the end to this `return false` and can never match anything. Consistent with "the language has no floats" — but a silent behaviour, not a diagnosed one.

excerpts.title: container_eq — the runtime's own deep equality

annotations.text: Mutual recursion with `raw_eq`, not with itself: nested SCALARS therefore get the language's typed equality (including the Account-vs-Str and Asset-vs-Str cross-type rules), which is precisely what `structural_equal`'s self-recursion does NOT do.

`l.t == r.t` means a Dict never equals an Obj even with identical fields, and the size check plus per-key lookup means the key SETS must match exactly while their order need not. Order is observable in neither comparator AND in neither dump — both renderers sort keys. Only `describe()` and the positional assertions in `DexRecordsTest.cpp` ever see it.

Cells compare by root hash on this path too, so a spec's `==` on two cells is a hash compare and never a byte compare — the same decision as the dump's cellhash rendering, taken independently in the runtime.

The catch-all: any mismatched pairing that reached here is simply unequal, never a fault. Faults in `==` come from two specific places above this (float-backed Amount, TON-asset vs string) — everything else degrades to false, which is what keeps a wrong-shaped guard from killing a match.

sections.heading: Truthiness: there isn't any
sections.prose:
Python's "empty list is false" has NO analogue in this engine. A matcher's `where` expression must evaluate to a genuine `Bool` that is `true`; the Walker's check is `!r.faulted && r.value.t == VType::Bool && r.value.boolean`, so a null, a zero Int, an empty List, or a faulted evaluation are all equally "did not match" ([[matcher-runtime]]). That single line is why null-propagation is safe: an expression that silently became null just fails the guard instead of throwing.

The one place a Python-ish truthiness is reproduced is inside a host function, over a block's data dict — and it is narrow on purpose.

excerpts.title: data_truthy — the only truthiness in the engine, and it is a host-side view

annotations.text: Only two kinds can be truthy: a `true` Bool and a non-zero Int. A missing field, a null, an empty string, an empty list — all false. It exists to mirror Python host code writing `if block.data.get("has_internal_transfer")` and is used by exactly one family of callers (the StonFi hosts), which is why it lives in `host/BlockViews.h` rather than in `Value.h`.

It goes through `data_field`, which returns a null Value for an absent field — so "absent" and "present but null" collapse here. That collapse is fine for a host predicate and would be wrong in the expression language, where a missing field faults ([[block-tree]] covers `Block::data`).

sections.heading: Check yourself
sections.prose:
Four things you can verify in a few minutes; each one pins a claim from this page.

1. THE NULL/ADDR_NONE SPLIT IS REAL, AND VISIBLE. Re-run the parse-dump command from the accounts section and grep for both spellings: `--parse-dump -T tests\traces | Select-String 'addr_none'` returns NOTHING over this corpus, while `response_address=null` and `response=null` are common. That is the pytoniq universe's answer to a missing address. Now read `AbiBridge.cpp`'s `adapt_address` ([[parse-layer]]) and confirm the ABI path would have printed `addr_none` for the same wire bytes.

2. THE BOC SET REALLY IS NAME-GATED, AND SHARED. `boc_field_names()` in `Value.cpp` lists seven names; `--surface` prints the same seven; `twins/cpp_surface.py` reads them as `BOC_FIELDS` out of the committed `cpp_surface.json`. Add a name to `boc_field_names()`, rebuild, then regenerate `cpp_surface.json` — both dumps change together. Skip the regen and the A/B gate goes red, which is the enforcement (nothing stops you from skipping it). Then confirm the exclusion: `comment` is a Bytes field and renders as `b64:…` in the dump, never as a cellhash.

3. THE TWO EQUALITIES ARE WIRED TO DIFFERENT CALLERS. `grep -rn structural_equal ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src` returns the declaration, the definition plus its two internal recursions, and exactly two external call sites — `VectorRunner.cpp:169` and `BuildVectorRunner.cpp:193`, both harness. `rt_eq` is called from `ExprEval.cpp:208` and `ClassifyCore.cpp:100`. Neither function ever calls the other.

4. FLOAT-BACKED AMOUNTS FAULT RATHER THAN COMPARE. The conformance vectors pin all three use sites (below). If you ever "fix" one of them to return null instead, expect `amount_float_eq_fault` to fail and the getgems A/B twin to diverge.
